paragraphs.context: Beneath the giant monster. The kid on his back, with the splintered
paragraphs.simple: Jack is the boy lying under the giant monster, holding a broken bat. He jokes that he is the good-looking kid who is about to be eaten.

paragraphs.context: Forty-two days ago, I was regular Jack Sullivan: thirteen years old
paragraphs.simple: Forty-two days ago Jack was a normal 13-year-old in a quiet, boring town called Wakefield. He was not a hero and did not fight monsters.

background.note: The made-up town where the story happens.

paragraphs.context: But look at me now. Battling a gargantuan beast on the roof
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is fighting a huge monster.
paragraphs.simple: Now Jack is fighting a giant beast on the roof of a shop.

background.note: A big chain of American shops that sell medicine and everyday things.

paragraphs.context: And me? I haven’t been normal, well, ever. I’ve always been different
paragraphs.simple: Jack is an orphan. He has lived with many families all over the country, and he came to Wakefield in December.

paragraphs.context: I’m at CVS because I need an eyeglass repair kit – those little
paragraphs.mainIdea: Why Jack went to the shop.
paragraphs.simple: Jack came to the shop for a glasses repair kit, because it has a tiny screwdriver. He needs it to fix his broken walkie-talkie.

paragraphs.context: It’s time to stop being this monster’s punching bag.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is tired of being hit. He feels the world has always treated him badly, so now he will fight.

paragraphs.context: I grip the bat in my hand.
paragraphs.simple: Jack holds his bat the way a baseball coach taught him: not too tight and not too loose.

background.note: A baseball league for children in America.

paragraphs.context: The monster’s massive hand snatches me out of mid-air.
paragraphs.simple: The monster catches Jack in the air. In its huge hand Jack is as small as a thimble.

paragraphs.context: I try to grab hold of my baseball bat blade (aka the
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants to use his sharp broken bat, but the monster holds his arms too tightly.

background.note: Jack's name for his broken bat. Louisville Slugger is a famous make of baseball bat.

paragraphs.context: He pulls me in close to his face.
paragraphs.simple: The monster pulls Jack close. Spit runs from its mouth and it breathes in his smell. Jack jokes that he is like the woman in King Kong, but this beast does not love him.

background.note: An old film about a giant ape that holds a woman in its hand.

paragraphs.context: None that felt this terrifyingly smart.
paragraphs.simple: The monster seems very clever. Jack feels deep inside that it is completely evil.

paragraphs.context: A smile seems to creep across the monster’s face.
paragraphs.simple: The monster seems to smile, as if it is saying that it is a great evil and will enjoy hurting Jack.

paragraphs.context: With a spine-tingling moan, the beast’s mouth opens wide, revealing an
paragraphs.simple: The monster opens its mouth to eat Jack. Jack kicks and twists and then bites its hand. The monster lets go a little, and Jack pulls his bat free.

paragraphs.context: I land in the junk-food aisle.
paragraphs.simple: Jack lands among the snacks and eats an old Oreo. Since the world ended, everything is free to take.

background.note: A popular chocolate biscuit with white cream inside.

paragraphs.context: One of the monster’s giant feet fills, like, the entire store.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The monster's foot fills the shop.
paragraphs.simple: The monster's foot is huge and fills the shop. Jack runs over it and finds the repair kit.

paragraphs.context: The monster’s clawed fingers tear through the roof like it’s nothing.
paragraphs.simple: The monster tears the roof open. Jack runs for the door. He jokes that he would like to stay and shop, but there is a giant monster.

paragraphs.context: I photograph every monster I come across, so later on I can
paragraphs.simple: Jack photographs every monster so he can study how they fight and what they are good and bad at. He also thinks it is cool.

paragraphs.context: I give each monster a name, too.
paragraphs.simple: Jack gives every monster a name. This one frightens him so much that his stomach feels mixed up.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly, there’s a racket like a wrecking ball crashing into ten million
paragraphs.simple: The shop falls down as Blarg walks through its walls. Now Jack sees how huge and tall Blarg really is.

paragraphs.context: Blarg turns and stomps his way down Spring Street, away from the
paragraphs.simple: Blarg walks away down the street, still smelling the ground like a dog. Jack knows Blarg has his smell now.

paragraphs.context: But I’m getting used to things being super way dangerous close.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is getting used to danger. Life after the monsters came is scary and strange, but Jack says he is strange too.

paragraphs.context: This is where I live. I know it’s not like a real
paragraphs.simple: Jack lives in the tree house. It has no bathroom or real windows, but he likes it.

paragraphs.context: The tree house used to belong to my scummy little foster brother.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house belonged to his nasty little foster brother. Jack has added a lot to it since the monsters came.

paragraphs.context: Now, why does a thirteen-year-old need a tree house that’s
paragraphs.simple: Jack asks why a 13-year-old needs a tree house stronger than the safest places in films.

background.note: A very well-guarded US army base where gold is kept.
Iron Man's building in Marvel films and comics.
The X-Men's house in Marvel comics and films.

paragraphs.context: Because a MASS of zombie hordes and monster brutes have taken over
paragraphs.simple: Huge crowds of zombies and big monsters now control Wakefield, and maybe the whole world.

paragraphs.context: Like the Dozers – big, hulking brutes that resemble two-legged rhinoceroses.
paragraphs.simple: Dozers are big, heavy monsters that look like rhinos walking on two legs.

paragraphs.context: And there are also the Vine-Thingies – long red vines that are alive.
paragraphs.simple: Vine-Thingies are long red plants that are alive and dangerous. They turn gardens into dangerous jungles.

paragraphs.context: It’s ’cause I think it’s important that future people know what it
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants people in the future to know what life was like after the monsters came.

paragraphs.context: Like I said, before the Monster Apocalypse I was an orphan.
paragraphs.simple: Jack was an orphan before the monsters came, and he still is.

paragraphs.context: The last family I got stuck with – the Robinsons – they were the worst.
paragraphs.simple: The Robinsons, his last foster family, were the worst. When the monsters came, they ran away and left him.

paragraphs.context: I wasn’t all that surprised they left me behind.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is not surprised that they left. He thinks they only took him in so he would clear up the leaves.

paragraphs.context: Now, if this sounds like I’m trying to make you feel bad
paragraphs.simple: Jack says he is not trying to make us feel sorry for him. He is just telling us the facts.

paragraphs.context: I learned a long time ago that it’s best to try not
paragraphs.simple: Jack has learned not to worry too much about bad things. When life tries to hit you, move out of the way and keep going. Someone else always has it worse.

paragraphs.context: Ever since the Robinsons peaced out – that’s forty-two days ago, now
paragraphs.simple: For forty-two days Jack has lived alone among monsters. He decides to treat life like a video game.

paragraphs.context: And that’s easy, because I’ve always looked at life from a video
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack has always thought like this.
paragraphs.simple: Jack has always seen life like a game, thinking of people's skills and of problems as big fights at the end of a level.

paragraphs.context: I earn them by completing goals and challenges.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wins a Feat when he does a challenge. The more dangerous it is, the better the Feat. He always needs a photo to prove it.

paragraphs.context: When I first moved to Wakefield, I decided I wanted to be
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wanted to take news photos.
paragraphs.simple: When Jack came to Wakefield, he decided to take photos for the news. He says it just means taking photos of exciting things.

paragraphs.context: So I was like, whatever, I’ll handle this on my own, and
paragraphs.simple: Jack got a job taking photos for the school newspaper. That is where he met June Del Toro.

paragraphs.context: June was the student editor of the Parker Middle School Gazette, which
paragraphs.simple: June was in charge of the school newspaper. Jack was happy, because working together gave them a reason to talk.

paragraphs.context: Turns out, though, June is scary when she’s on the job.
paragraphs.simple: June is scary when she is working, but Jack still thinks she is very cute.

paragraphs.context: She told me I was lazy.
paragraphs.simple: June said Jack was lazy. Jack says he was just playing the part of the cool photographer who does things his own way.

paragraphs.context: June said my photos weren’t capturing the important stories around the school.
paragraphs.simple: June said Jack's photos missed the important school stories. Jack thinks she just wanted boring photos.

paragraphs.context: See, I don’t go in for a lot of that boring junk.
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not like boring things. He likes to catch an exciting moment that will never happen again.

paragraphs.context: And now? Now my camera is full of once-in-a-lifetime
paragraphs.simple: Now his camera is full of photos of very dangerous moments.

paragraphs.context: The day the Monster Apocalypse began I know FOR A FACT June
paragraphs.simple: Jack is sure June was in the school when the monsters came. But when he went back and shouted her name, nobody answered.

paragraphs.context: I’m also VERY SURE that June’s parents did not leave town, because
paragraphs.simple: Jack is also sure June's parents did not leave town. Their cars are still at their house, and it does not look as if they packed and left.

paragraphs.context: I’m a dorky warrior orphan. I’m a zombie-fighting, monster-slaying tornado
paragraphs.simple: Jack calls himself a silly orphan warrior who fights zombies and monsters. He promises to rescue June and finish his biggest Feat.

paragraphs.context: It’s dusk and the sun is setting, all orange like a Popsicle.
paragraphs.simple: The sun is going down. Orange light shines into the tree house, and a little wind chime rings.

paragraphs.context: I’m huddled over the busted walkie, trying to repair it with my
paragraphs.simple: Jack bends over his broken walkie-talkie and tries to fix it with the tiny screwdriver.

paragraphs.context: When I first moved to Wakefield last winter, Quint was the only
paragraphs.simple: When Jack came to Wakefield, Quint was the only kid who talked to him. Foster kids who move a lot get used to having no friends.

paragraphs.context: Quint gave me the walkie – one half of a pair – for my birthday.
paragraphs.simple: Quint gave Jack one of a pair of walkies for his birthday. Jack had no phone, and Quint's parents thought phones were bad for your brain, so the walkies were how they talked.

paragraphs.context: But now I’m afraid Quint is gone.
paragraphs.simple: On the day it all happened, they went different ways. Jack fears that Quint is now a zombie or has gone west with everyone else.

paragraphs.context: Seven finger burns later, I get the walkie working.
paragraphs.simple: After burning his fingers seven times, Jack gets the walkie working. It makes a soft sound to show it is sending.

paragraphs.context: School was almost over and everyone had that summertime fever feeling – like
paragraphs.mainIdea: The end of the school year.
paragraphs.simple: School was almost over and everyone felt summer coming. Jack was not so happy, because summer meant more time with the Robinsons and lots of grass-cutting.

paragraphs.context: I remember, too, that Quint was eating this rotten-smelling egg salad sandwich.
paragraphs.simple: Quint was eating an egg sandwich that smelled terrible. Jack can still remember the smell.

paragraphs.context: Dirk Savage was the most formidable bully at Parker Middle School.
paragraphs.simple: Dirk was the scariest bully in the school. Kids told a story that his parents ran away from him and he lived alone in a hut in the woods.

paragraphs.context: Dirk snatched the sandwich from Quint’s hand and jammed the thing – which
paragraphs.simple: Dirk grabbed Quint's sandwich and pushed it into his own mouth.

paragraphs.context: But it wasn’t fine. I hate jerks – whether they’re monster jerks or
paragraphs.simple: But Jack hates mean people of every kind, human or monster.

paragraphs.context: I turned back to Dirk. ‘Maybe a very rotund panda bear? That
paragraphs.simple: Jack joked that Dirk should pick on a fat panda bear his own size.

paragraphs.context: ‘I do. But to be fair, I also think people slipping on
paragraphs.simple: Jack said he thinks lots of silly things are funny, like people falling on ice.

paragraphs.context: It was a scream of pure horror.
paragraphs.simple: This scream was full of fear. Dirk let Jack go, and Jack looked out of the window.

paragraphs.context: Next there was a Godzilla-sounding howl, like REARGHHHH!!!, and the whole
paragraphs.simple: A huge roar came, and the bus suddenly moved. The boys were thrown about, and the driver cried like a baby.

paragraphs.context: The monster tilted the bus so the back pointed toward the sky.
paragraphs.simple: The monster lifted the back of the bus. All the kids fell down to the front.

paragraphs.context: ‘Quint?’ I managed. I could barely breathe. Kids all over me. An
paragraphs.simple: Jack was squashed under other kids and could hardly breathe. He asked Quint what was happening.

paragraphs.context: This monster’s hulking paw squeezed the bus like it was an empty
paragraphs.simple: The monster squeezed the bus and the door opened. The kids fell out onto the ground. Jack's nose bled, but he got up and pulled Quint away from the crowd.

paragraphs.context: June turned, dodged the stumbling, falling zombie, left it sprawled out on
paragraphs.simple: June turned, got away from the zombie and ran into the school. She and Jack looked at each other, and then the door shut.

paragraphs.context: I said to myself then that whatever happened, whatever came next, somehow
paragraphs.simple: Jack promised himself that one day he would go back to the school and find June.

paragraphs.context: And we did. We sprinted away from the school bus and the
paragraphs.simple: The boys ran away from the bus, the monster and the zombies, over the fence and into the woods.

paragraphs.context: ‘Quint,’ I said, catching my breath and pulling him behind a tree.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said they needed to find somewhere safe, or that heroes from films should come and help.

background.note: A team of soldier heroes from toys and cartoons.
A team of Marvel superheroes.
A Marvel superhero in a metal suit.

paragraphs.context: Quint groaned. ‘My parents are on vacation. I have a babysitter. I’ll
paragraphs.simple: Quint's parents were away. He would go home and see what to do, and Jack should go to his house.

paragraphs.context: ‘Deal.’ I was trying to stay calm, be classic cool Jack Sullivan
paragraphs.simple: Jack agreed. He tried to act cool, but his heart was beating fast and his body was shaking.

paragraphs.context: I climbed up into the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: In the tree house, Jack fell onto the table in panic and knocked the walkie out of the door.

paragraphs.context: I stared at the walkie on the ground below.
paragraphs.simple: Jack needed the walkie, but he was too scared to climb down and get it.

paragraphs.context: It got worse. Zombies everywhere. Giant monsters on the horizon. I blacked
paragraphs.simple: There were zombies everywhere and monsters in the distance. Jack covered the windows and stayed inside.

paragraphs.context: There was an old AM/FM radio in the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: At first the radio said it was safer in the west. After five days the radio stopped.

paragraphs.context: When I finally worked up the courage to go out and do
paragraphs.simple: After nine days, Jack was brave enough to go out and look around.

paragraphs.context: I leap to my feet. Almost. One leg is asleep. I fall
paragraphs.simple: Jack jumps up so fast that he falls, hurts his knee and hits his head, but he gets to the walkie.

paragraphs.context: Could the zombies and the monsters have started to talk ?
paragraphs.simple: Jack wonders if the zombies have learned to talk and are using Quint's voice to trick him.

paragraphs.context: I’m so relieved my best (only) friend is alive that I don’t
paragraphs.simple: Jack is so glad Quint is alive that he does not tease him about his strange favourite food.

paragraphs.context: That’s how Quint talks. He fancies himself a scientist, so apparently that
paragraphs.simple: Quint thinks he is a scientist, so he talks like an old man from long ago.

paragraphs.context: I smile. Ear to ear. Literally, the corner of my lip is
paragraphs.simple: Jack smiles very widely. He says Quint's words are the best he has ever heard.

paragraphs.context: Last week, while exploring the library, I found an old map of
paragraphs.simple: Jack found an old map of the town. He put it on the board and wrote notes about important places and monsters.

paragraphs.context: I plot a route to Quint’s, then I suit up.
paragraphs.simple: Jack plans his way to Quint's house and puts on his fighting clothes. They are not very good; they look like a Halloween costume.

paragraphs.context: I mostly use this busted baseball bat – the one I got Blarg
paragraphs.simple: Jack's main weapon is his broken bat. It is sharp now, so he calls it the Louisville Slicer.

paragraphs.context: The zombies used to be people!
paragraphs.simple: Zombies used to be people. It is not their fault, so Jack will not stab them.

paragraphs.context: So for zombie-fighting, I use a busted old hockey stick.
paragraphs.simple: For zombies, Jack uses an old hockey stick. He just hits them on the head and keeps going.

paragraphs.context: My foster mom gave me these hand-me-down shoes called Light-Upz.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's foster mother gave him old shoes with red lights that flash when you walk. They are really for very young children.

paragraphs.context: At school, stupid Nick DeRobertis told me that his cousin Silvio DeRobertis’s
paragraphs.mainIdea: A silly story about the shoes.
paragraphs.simple: A boy at school told Jack a silly story about someone who got hurt by electricity from these shoes in a puddle.

paragraphs.context: So I wrapped the shoes in duct tape so you can’t see the lights.
paragraphs.simple: So Jack covered the shoes with tape. They look ugly, but they are safe.

paragraphs.context: Anyway, Quint is like a super genius, so I’m hoping he can
paragraphs.simple: Quint is very clever, so Jack hopes he can make Jack's gear much better.

background.note: A film about a police officer who is turned into a robot.

paragraphs.context: I make it almost all the way to Quint’s house just by
paragraphs.simple: Jack gets almost to Quint's house by moving quietly through gardens. But Oak Street is full of zombies.

paragraphs.context: I decide to hop the fence and go across the football field
paragraphs.simple: Jack decides to cross the football field. Open fields are dangerous, but going round would take too long and he is excited to see Quint.

paragraphs.context: I’m in a real pickle. And I hate pickles . I hate pickles
paragraphs.simple: Jack is in real trouble between two Dozers. He jokes about the word "pickle" and about jam.

paragraphs.context: First, an old-man zombie – he’s got one eyeball dangling out, and
paragraphs.simple: The first zombie is an old man with one eye hanging out. He jumps at Jack.

paragraphs.context: I dive under his outstretched hands.
paragraphs.simple: Jack goes under the old man's hands and meets a very old woman zombie. She grabs his shirt, but he gets free.

paragraphs.context: I leap off the picnic table, using one zombie’s bald, mouldy head
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack uses a zombie as a step.
paragraphs.simple: Jack jumps off a table, steps on a zombie's bald head and grabs the tyre swing.

paragraphs.context: Quint yanks open the sliding door just as a hulking, half-rotten
paragraphs.mainIdea: A big zombie at the door.
paragraphs.simple: Quint opens the door, but a huge, half-rotten zombie stands in front of it.

paragraphs.context: Quint slams the patio door shut behind me.
paragraphs.simple: Quint shuts the glass door just in time. Three zombies bump into the glass and fall back, like in a silly comedy.

paragraphs.context: ‘Um, yeah. Remember?! We worked on it that whole afternoon one time
paragraphs.simple: Jack reminds Quint about the secret handshake they once planned, so people would think they had cool secrets.

paragraphs.context: On the way upstairs, I pull out my list of Feats and
paragraphs.simple: On the way upstairs Jack ticks a Feat on his list: reaching Quint's house alive.

paragraphs.context: Quint’s house – the same house where I spent almost every day after
paragraphs.simple: Jack spent almost every day here for six months, but now it feels different, and he cannot say why.

paragraphs.context: ‘This is all research. I’ve learned much about our foes. It looks
paragraphs.simple: Quint has been studying the monsters and has started putting them into groups, like a scientist.

paragraphs.context: Quint continues, ‘I’m about to begin classifying the monsters by genus and
paragraphs.simple: Quint plans to sort the monsters into scientific groups and give marks for their skills.

paragraphs.context: Quint is silent for a moment.
paragraphs.simple: Quint's parents were away on holiday. He does not know where they are, but he hopes they are safe in the west.

paragraphs.context: I cough into my hand and say, ‘Hey, Quint.
paragraphs.simple: Jack asks if it is true that the monsters came to the east first and that the army in the west was ready to stop them.

paragraphs.context: Quint looks up at the ceiling.
paragraphs.simple: Quint only knows what he can see: monsters and zombies everywhere and very few people alive. The internet and phones do not work.

paragraphs.context: Quint shakes his head. ‘Absolutely not. Safest option is to stay here
paragraphs.simple: Quint thinks it is safest to stay in a safe place and wait for help.

paragraphs.context: Finally, I stand up and say, trying to sound cheerful, ‘Let’s split, bud.
paragraphs.simple: Jack tries to sound happy. He tells Quint to come to the tree house, which is much better now.

paragraphs.context: He flicks the light switch and what I see – man, I have
paragraphs.simple: Quint turns on the light in the garage. Jack is amazed: there is a cool truck made for the end of the world.

paragraphs.context: ‘Now pay attention, Jack,’ he says, and he begins detailing the truck’s
paragraphs.simple: Quint shows all the machines on the truck. Jack thinks a clever kid can do a lot when nobody tells him to do homework.

paragraphs.context: We spend the next hour stuffing all of Quint’s research and equipment
paragraphs.simple: They pack Quint's research and toys into the truck. Then Quint asks if Jack knows how to drive.

paragraphs.context: ‘So I’ve played like two hundred hours of Need for Speed !
paragraphs.simple: Jack says he has played a driving video game for hundreds of hours, so of course he can drive.

background.note: A car-racing video game.

paragraphs.context: We get back to the tree house with no major issues.
paragraphs.simple: The drive is mostly fine. A crowd of zombies makes Jack drive past the broken shop.

paragraphs.context: And now I’ll use his mega-smart science brain to help me
paragraphs.simple: Jack plans to use Quint's clever brain to help him find June.

paragraphs.context: Quint is definitely type numero uno.
paragraphs.simple: Quint is the first kind. Every day he gets up very early to study the end of the world like a scientist.

paragraphs.context: On the plus side, Quint is a big fan of my photos
paragraphs.simple: Quint likes Jack's photos because they help him study the monsters. He does not see them as art.

paragraphs.context: The problem is that all this research keeps reminding me that IT’S
paragraphs.simple: All this research reminds Jack how frightening the world outside is.

paragraphs.context: Tomorrow, I’m going to be all Liam Neeson-y, like, ‘WHAT’S UP, ZOMBIES?!
paragraphs.simple: Tomorrow Jack will be tough, like a hero in an action film.

background.note: An actor famous for playing tough men who rescue people.

paragraphs.context: Tomorrow, bright and early, we’re scouring this town for June.
